rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 4.1, 5.1 <U+2013> own field evaluations of basin irrigation events at Pingluo (flume inflow rates, advance/recession, infiltrometer tests, Tables 3, 6, 7) plus own SRFR/ISAREG simulation runs. Q2: Sections 4.2, 6.2, Tables 8, 11, 12 <U+2013> the authors apply the ISAREG water-balance model, with the Stewart yield-water equation (Eq. 4) and the Ayers-Westcot salinity equation (Eq. 3) combined (Eqs. 5-9), to search improved irrigation schedules that save 21-30% water on non-saline soils and 8-22% on saline soils while applying leaching fractions; Section 5.2 notes simulated present-condition values are similar to those observed in field evaluations and SRFR was calibrated on observed advance/recession (Fig. 4). Q4: Tables 8, 11, 12 and Fig. 7 <U+2013> the model computes percolation, capillary rise, available soil water and leaching depths, i.e. the intermediate variables through which scheduling controls salinity and saves water. Q7: end of Section 6.2 and Conclusions <U+2013> savings are stated to be achievable only under condition that upstream diversions are reduced so drainage functions, the drainage system is upgraded to lower the water table below 1 m, precision zero leveling and higher inflow rates are adopted, and delivery scheduling is adapted; farmers cannot improve without support. Q8: Section 4.2 <U+2013> a mechanistic model would be required to properly simulate salt dynamics, the salinity subroutine is a simplification; Section 5.2 <U+2013> despite model accuracy some uncertainty remains in simulated percolation/capillary rise; Section 3.2 <U+2013> insufficient information on salinity effects of under-irrigation.
rows.notes: The improved scheduling results (Tables 11, 12) are model scenarios, not measured outcomes; validation is indirect (ISAREG validated elsewhere, SRFR calibrated on observed advance/recession, present-condition simulations said to resemble field observations), so Q2 is answered yes on the descriptive claim that the study applies Eq. 3 with a simulation model to search schedules under salinity and water scarcity, but the water-saving magnitudes are unverified. Q3: field data only parameterise the models; no independent second method confirms the scheduling result. Q5: results given for wheat, maize and the wheat-maize intercrop but at one site (Pingluo, HID), one soil TAW class and one district; intercrop is a combination of the same two crops, so representativeness judged insufficient (doubt). Q6: field/basin scale only; district-scale use is referred to other papers. Q9: ranges in Table 7 and SD in Table 3 concern current field performance and geometry, not the improved-schedule result; the 25-40% savings range is a scenario range, not dispersion.

notes: Full text available including tables; figures described in captions only. The study combines own field evaluations with SRFR and ISAREG simulations for the Huinong Irrigation District, Ningxia.
